name: The Pigeonhole Principle
statement: More pigeons than holes means at least two must share a hole.
statementAccent: at least two must share a hole
meaning: If you put more items into containers than there are containers, at least one container must hold more than one item. More objects than boxes forces sharing — it is simply impossible to give every object its own box.
mechanism: The principle is almost self-evidently true yet powerfully non-constructive: it proves that a collision must exist without identifying which container is crowded or which items collide. That is the source of its power in existence proofs — you establish that something exists without ever exhibiting it. The generalised form sharpens it: with n items in m boxes, some box holds at least the ceiling of n over m.

examples.text: Among 367 people at least two must share a birthday, since there are only 366 possible dates — a certainty, unlike the merely probable match at 23.
Since a human head has at most about a million hairs and a large city has more people than that, at least two residents must have exactly the same number of hairs.
Distribute more than a multiple of m items among m boxes and some box must hold more than that multiple — the counting version used throughout combinatorics.

variants.name: The birthday problem
variants.text: The probabilistic cousin: where the pigeonhole principle guarantees a shared birthday at 367 people, the birthday problem asks how likely one is, and finds better-than-even odds at just 23.

variants.name: Ramsey theory
variants.text: The far-reaching generalisation about unavoidable structure — that any sufficiently large system must contain some order — of which the pigeonhole principle is the simplest case.

whyItMatters: It is one of the most useful tools in combinatorics and computer science, proving that collisions and coincidences are unavoidable — from hash collisions to compression limits — with a one-line argument. Its non-constructive power, guaranteeing existence without location, makes it a favourite in elegant proofs.

working.text: when items outnumber the possible categories, conclude that some category must be shared, without needing to find which.
for a guaranteed concentration, note that some box holds at least the ceiling of items over boxes.
having proved a collision must exist, remember you still have to locate it if you need the specific items.

limits: It is a proven, elementary theorem with no evidential limitation — it admits no counterexamples and needs no assumptions. Its only genuine constraint is conceptual: it is existence-only, guaranteeing that a collision exists but not where or which items collide, so locating the collision requires additional work. It must also not be confused with the birthday problem: pigeonhole gives a guarantee at 367 people, the birthday problem a probability at 23 — different questions entirely.
misreadings: It tells you a shared category must exist, not which one — it is non-constructive, proving existence without identity. And it is not the birthday problem: the birthday problem is about likelihood at small group sizes, while the pigeonhole principle is a hard guarantee once items exceed categories.
origin: Commonly called Dirichlet's box principle after Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet's 1834 use of it under the name 'Schubfachprinzip', though this is a naming convention rather than first discovery — an earlier written statement appears in Jean Leurechon's work of 1622.
